Worked in masonry for many years. While pretty much any construction method can be Googled, actual bricklaying involves a lot of careful finesse that can only come with practice. Each brick must have the right amount of mortar applied, and placed correctly within less than a 1/16 inch margin of error. If you're off, you have a few seconds to gently tap the brick in the right place. After that, enough moisture is pulled out of the mortar, and any movement will break the bond. You'd have to pull the brick and start over.

I recommend you start with a small practice mound, which you can easily tear down and start over until you feel you're comfortable enough laying brick.

Traditional brick construction, not an owner-builder's friend. As Sippio pointed out, there's significant skill involved and it really takes hands-on learning. There are trade schools for this if you want to go into it as a profession, but for the owner-built house it's not the smartest choice. In the US brick construction has become very rare because it's just too high in labor, and labor is the largest portion of the cost of home construction. This is what drove the transition here from brick to stick-frame use after it was introduced in the Chicago area in the late 19th century as a gimmick to increase the sales of small dimension lumber. However, there are some brick-like alternatives with much lower skill requirements, depending on where you want to to build and the kind of material you're willing to work with.

Traditional adobe block construction has enjoyed a revival thanks to the green building movement. Adobe blocks are made of clay-bearing earth and straw made into a soft mud formed in wood frames and air dried. The earthen material is sometimes combined with a binding agent.(native Americans actually used cactus juice but today things like cement or asphalt are used) Though still requiring some skill, it's not as difficult as working with fired brick because adobe blocks are much larger, the adobe mortar used is very thin, and the walls are very thick. So it doesn't require quite as much precision. However, adobe relies heavily on an exterior 'rendering'--the smooth adobe covering applied to the outside--to protect the blocks, which needs to be renewed frequently. If you keep room sizes modest and your building to just one story, adobe buildings are really simple and strong. You don't need an additional wood frame. You just build the walls and top them with a cement bond-beam and roof trusses or--more traditionally--just thick wood beams or peeled log 'vigas' embedded in the adobe that support the ceiling made of 'latilla' (basically sticks laid in patterns over the vigas or beams) and a flat compound roof. Of course, use of flat roofs tends to be limited to dryer climate areas. With more modern roofing, this construction can work in most any environment.

The successor to adobe is Compressed Earth Block. This is a block made of earth with a small amount of cement that is compressed in a machine originally called a 'cinva ram'. Compressed earth blocks are more resilient than adobe (making surface rendering optional), have higher load bearing strength, and are often made in forms that give them lego-like block shapes that interlock so they can achieve better bonds and form more uniform walls with less skill. They are used to build simple homes in basically the same way as adobe but they have the versatility of fired brick allowing for creation of more complex structures like arches. CEB is very popular for both green housing, relief housing, and use in the developing world. The traditional cinva rams were simple hand-powered machines but the labor for that was so high that they soon became mechanized and there are many such machines now. The Open Source Ecology organization has developed open source plans for a CEB machine which you can see here. The most sophisticated CEB mold system is the one developed for the Auram CEB machines developed in Auroville India. They have many different forms to produce a large variety of special-purpose blocks that save a lot of construction labor. Auroville--a religious community--uses these machines for much of its architecture and has produce some of the most beautiful earthen buildings in the world. But you can only buy these machines in India.

The origin of adobe construction is 'cob' construction, which is based on stacking up loafs of soft clay-rich earth in courses to form walls and then hand-sculpting them into the desired shape. Though a more sculptural process, it's not high skill and most people can learn the techniques quickly. If a building cannot be built at once, care must be taken to keep unfinished courses of building moist and in general this limits buildings to relatively small sizes so they can be completed in modest amounts of time. You really have to be able to finish the walls of a home in a building season. Once the walls are dried, an adobe-like rendering is applied and roofing built in much the same way as adobe, though traditional construction will employ a thatched roof. Cob houses usually have a very wide roof overhang to protect the walls from rain This is a very ancient yet perfectly practical building method that has a long tradition among both native Americans and ancient Europeans. To this day cob buildings are used in the UK. With the rise of interest in green building in the 1980s, there was a revival of cob building techniques originating in Oregon US that has spread across the world. Many of the 'hobbit style' homes you see pictures of today are cob buildings.

In Mexico there is a Mennonite community that often employs formed concrete or soil-cement (a mixture of soil and cement) construction. But they often want the appearance of brick construction so they made steel forms that mimic the look of brick. Soil-cement is one of the lowest-labor forms of earthen construction. (the next lowest-labor type the Super-Adobe method devised by Nader Khalili) It is used for buildings in the same style as adobe but with rendering optional because of the high cement content. I currently live in a cottage in New Mexico that was made with a combination of adobe and soil-cement construction.

Earthen construction methods are extremely popular for green architecture and there are countless books and web sites about them. There are also many places offering training, but IMO these can sometimes be a bit of a scam. Earth building methods are still very labor intensive. Even if it's low skill, it's not something really suited to someone working alone unless they want to spend 5 years building house. And hiring builders for this is very expensive because it's considered 'unconventional'. So green architects will often run classes in earthen building just so they can get the free labor to build things. These people then go to apply their skills to their own homes only to discover they can't handle the labor. So they, in turn, start running classes to teach the methods so they can get their own free labor. It often seems a little like a Ponzie scheme to me.

In Europe there are a variety of extruded corrugated modular clay block systems. Factory-made with high precision, they often feature interlocking shapes and very light weight and are assembled using only thin-set mortar applied in horizontal courses rather like glue, often using a mechanical roller to 'paint' the surface of each course. Mostly used as non-load-bearing curtain walls, some of these block systems feature very large unit blocks with a honeycomb interior and channels for steel reinforcement that will suit load-bearing walls. But these systems tend to need a lot surface finishing work to produce a nice looking structure and they're proprietary--which means that if the company goes out of business you have no place to get new blocks when you need something repaired.

There are also a number of modular cast stone block building systems, popular for upper-class homes and monumental construction because they are designed to mimic the look of classic cut stone construction. These use precision-made prefinished interlocking blocks, sometimes with built-in foam insulation, that are dry-stacked and permanently bonded by filling channels with rebar and poured concrete. It's quite a simple method of construction and extremely strong, but very expensive. One system I know of was developed in Texas and intented to immitate everything from Italiante architecture to the traditional Texas limestone houses. Though suggested for DIY use, these block are really big and heavy and usually need some kind of mechanical assistance to safely move and position them.

Unfortunately, if you're alone and want to build a house in less than 5 years, there probably isn't a way to use any kind of brick construction. It's just too heavy, too labor intensive. There is, actually, a life-size form of lego blocks now available, but this could only be used for permanent housing in combination with steel frame construction.

It is exactly respect for democracy. What this article fails to mention is that this isn't a push by the government, it is a push by the people of California. For a few years now groups around the country have been trying to raise the minimum wage various ways to various levels in various places, with the overall theme of Fight for Fifteen.

A few places have done some work, but in California, it was not to the satisfaction of the general populous. State law allows ballot initiatives for people to directly represent themselves in the legislative process as a check/balance in the government. This is how we recalled our failed governor (the first in U.S. history I think), it is how Prop 8 got passed, and it was about to be how the minimum wage got push to 15$.

After failing to meet the people's wants and needs, the people put together a ballot initiative, got enough signatures and we were going to vote on it come the next elections. The new law did not mince words, it basically said, effective immediately, phased in over 5 years, the minimum wage would be 15$ for all workers, no exceptions, and there would be annual increases based on the CPI (Inflation). Currently, there are a number of exceptions (air carrier workers, union contracts, etc.) Right after the ballot initiative was certified for the next elections (nov 8th), business groups started issue statements about how they would like this to be done through the legislative process currently taking place and that they want to work with the Ballot's sponsor's to make this happen. Only the people who submitted the new law can withdraw it, and the legislative process they were referring to was STARTED in 2014 and wasn't going anywhere.

So yeah, that's how that happened, and why Gov Brown was not super happy to sign the bill. Now, whether it is good or bad as a whole in the end is being hashed out in this study and that opinion of this expert, but we probably won't know for some time. So far as the consequences, in this instance, they are a risk the people want to take and it is their right to do so.
